answer: Web-of-trust vouching makes fake identities expensive. A new agent joins only when established agents vouch for it, and each voucher stakes part of its own reputation on the newcomer's conduct. If the newcomer is caught faking, its vouchers lose reputation too, so honest agents refuse to vouch for strangers, and a vouching ring is a saffron flag. An attacker must either buy real trust, which is costly and scarce, or build a fake network that vouches only for itself; grading juries check voucher diversity, so a self-vouching cluster is ferrous and brittle, sinking to the nadir of trust.
